summary_plain: The Cool Flames Investigation burned liquid fuel droplets like n-dodecane and iso-dodecane mixtures in the microgravity environment of the International Space Station. Researchers studied how these cool flames behave at different pressures and oxygen levels to better understand low-temperature combustion chemistry. This research helps improve spacecraft fire safety by providing data on fuel flammability and droplet extinction in space.
summary_expert: CFI (PSI-39) ran 87 tests using the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The investigation tested droplet fuels including C12H26, [.60]/[.40] C12H26/iso-dodecane, and [.75]/[.25] C12H26/iso-dodecane, utilizing sample geometries of droplets and droplets on fibers. The oxygen concentration ranged from 17 to 21 percent (mole fraction 0.17 to 0.21), ambient pressures ranged from 51 to 507 kPa (0.50 to 5.00 atm), and diluent or suppressant gases included He and N2, while variables such as oxygen, pressure, fuel, diluent, and geometry were changed between tests.

key_findings.text: CFI (PSI-39) ran 87 tests according to its PSI experimental table.
The oxygen concentration in CFI tests ranged from 17 to 21 percent (mole fraction 0.17 to 0.21).
The ambient pressure in CFI tests ranged from 51 to 507 kPa (0.50 to 5.00 atm).

earth_applications: Design of advanced engines such as clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines
Development of new computational models to compute combustion performance in practical applications
Understanding of how cool flame reactivity determines octane and cetane number for fuels in spark ignition and diesel engines
